analysis.one_liner: Banned unregulated 'soft money' in federal campaigns, limited PAC money, and tightened disclosure of election ads.
analysis.headline: The bill won majority support in three separate Senate votes (53-47, 52-47, 52-47) in October 1997 but never reached the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster, and it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal campaign finance law. It banned national parties from raising or spending unlimited 'soft money' from corporations, unions, and big individual donors; barred most PAC contributions; required fast public reporting of independent ad spending; strengthened the foreign-money ban; banned using campaign funds for personal expenses; and stopped fundraising on federal property. In exchange it raised some individual contribution limits and offered compliant Senate candidates broadcast discounts and lower postage. Every Democrat and a few Republicans supported moving the bill, but opponents used the filibuster — the rule that lets 41 senators block a final vote — to stop it, winning three times despite the bill winning majorities each time.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for the candidates on their ballot. The bill would have made party committees fund federal campaigns only with disclosed, limited money, required near-real-time reporting of late-breaking political ads, banned foreign money, banned fundraising on federal property, and stopped members from converting campaign funds to personal use. Vulnerable incumbents would also have gained cheaper ads and postage if they accepted spending limits.

how_it_helps.text: It banned national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending 'soft money' — unlimited contributions from corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals that federal law does not limit or disclose — the largest legal channel for special-interest money into federal elections.

It required anyone spending more than $10,000 on election-related activity to report it, with 24- to 48-hour reporting for ads run in the final weeks, and imposed 'stand by your ad' disclosure requirements naming who paid for political advertising.

It banned contributions by political action committees, capped PAC money at 20% of a candidate's funds if a ban were not in effect, and stopped federal officeholders from raising unregulated money for state parties.

It strengthened the ban on foreign money, banned contributions from minors, barred fundraising on federal property (including by the President and Members of Congress), and banned the personal use of campaign funds.

It let Senate candidates who limit their own spending qualify for discounted broadcast time and reduced postage, and it stopped candidates from financing entire campaigns with personal wealth in exchange for party coordinated spending.

It tightened enforcement: higher penalties for knowing violations, random post-election audits, injunction power for the Federal Election Commission, and expedited procedures for complaints filed near an election.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees, which would lose unlimited soft money; PACs, which would lose the right to give; and large donors, unions, and corporations, who would have to give through limited, disclosed channels. Senators of both parties would lose the soft-money pipeline their campaign operations drew on.

drawbacks.text: The bill allowed each individual to give $30,000 a cycle, up from $25,000, and allowed donors up to $10,000 more to state party committees, so it loosened some limits even as it closed the soft-money loophole.
The ban on PAC contributions, while limiting big-money committee influence, would also have cut off a channel that labor unions and membership groups used to pool small donations from working people.

Defining 'express advocacy' with a fixed list of phrases and a 60-day window meant wealthy groups could still run 'issue ads' naming candidates outside that window or without those phrases, so the bill might not have stopped the flood of unregulated advertising it aimed at.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — closing the soft-money loophole, disclosure of late ad spending, a ban on PAC money — directly served voters' interest in knowing who funds their elections and shrinking the special-interest channel into the parties. The costs are real: the soft-money ban reduced party funds for voter registration and turnout, the express-advocacy test was narrow enough that big money could have shifted into issue ads, and critics questioned the constitutionality of regulating campaign spending. But the core trade — modest limits on how political parties and big givers fund federal campaigns, in exchange for cleaner elections — was one a Senate majority supported and was denied even a final vote.

outcome.mechanism: In October 1997 the Senate debated the bill, but a filibuster held: three cloture votes to end debate and let it come to a final vote got majorities (52-47, 53-47, 52-47) yet fell short of the 60 needed, so the bill was returned to the calendar and never voted on.

narrative.text: Senator McCain introduced S. 25 on January 21, 1997 with 31 cosponsors, 30 of them Democrats.
The Rules and Administration Committee discharged the bill by unanimous consent on September 25, 1997 and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
In late September and early October 1997 the Senate took the bill up by unanimous consent; Senator Lott moved to recommit it to the Rules Committee and offered an amendment.
On October 7, cloture on the Lott amendment failed 52-48, with 52 Republicans in favor and all 45 Democrats opposed.

On October 7, 8, and 9, three votes to end debate on the bill itself each got a majority — 53-47, 52-47, and 52-47 — with every Democrat and a handful of Republicans in favor, but each fell short of the 60 votes required.
A second cloture vote on the Lott amendment also failed 51-48 on October 9.
On October 30, 1997 the bill was returned to the calendar, and no final Senate vote was ever taken; only a subcommittee hearing on it was held in February 1998.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The national parties, large donors, and PACs kept the unlimited soft-money system intact; senators of both parties kept the fundraising system they relied on.

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the floor effort to end debate.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its namesake Democratic partner.

for.name: 45 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously to cut off debate on all three cloture votes so the bill could get a final vote.

for.name: 8 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to vote for cloture on the bill, including on the 53-47 vote.

against.name: 47 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cutting off debate on all three cloture votes, keeping the bill from an up-or-down vote.

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee and offered an amendment (SP 1258) that became the vehicle for delay during floor debate.

against.name: Party fundraising operations and donor networks of both parties
against.what_they_did: Both parties relied heavily on soft money for congressional campaigns, and members of both parties who benefited from it resisted the ban.

sides.party_line_note: On the key cloture votes, every Democrat (45 of 45) voted to end debate while 47 of 55 Republicans voted to keep the bill from a final vote; only 7-8 Republicans crossed over, though Republican McCain led the bill.

industries.note: The parties' largest funding stream — unlimited soft money from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors — would have been cut off, costing both parties hundreds of millions in a presidential cycle.
PACs would have been banned from federal contributions entirely, or limited to individual-level amounts if the ban lapsed.

industries.industry: Corporate and union treasuries and large individual donors
industries.note: The bill's core purpose was to shut the unregulated money channel these donors used to influence federal elections; their spending would have moved under limits and public disclosure.
Complying Senate candidates would get broadcast discounts and free time, cutting into ad revenue, and stations would face new 'stand by your ad' and disclosure requirements.
